Forecast vs. actual

The projection I built at feasibility, set against what the business actually did through mid-April. Reading the gap is the point.

$ForecastActualVariance
Units sold15048−102
Revenue7,2002,304−4,896
COGS3,637.51,411.2−2,226.3
Gross profit3,562.5892.9−2,669.6

The forecast assumed 50 units a month. Actual demand ramped slower and was affected by a mid-cycle supplier switch (see next section), so volume came in under plan. The contribution margin per unit held near $23.75, so gross profit stayed positive even at lower volume.

03

The pivot: a cost-quality squeeze

The value proposition was specific: better quality than the campus bookstore, at a lower price. A mid-cycle supplier change put that at risk, and the finance side had to price the trade-off.

What happened

New tariffs on China forced us off our original supplier mid-cycle. The fast replacement dropped fabric weight from 520gsm to 330gsm, closer to a bookstore basic than a premium hoodie, and added roughly $2 per shirt.

That put our whole positioning at risk: pay more, deliver less. Demand could fall even with a lower price.

What I weighed

I framed it as a margin-vs-positioning decision rather than a panic. We sourced a 450gsm supplier that held quality near the original spec while keeping unit cost workable, and re-ran the model to confirm the contribution margin still cleared break-even.

SpecRushedChosen
Fabric weight330 gsm450 gsm
PositioningAt riskHeld

On the operations side, I helped stand up a Square POS and a receipt-tracking system so every sale was logged in real time. That was the control layer that made the weekly reporting trustworthy, and the tie between the marketing funnel and the financial model.

05

Proceeds

Off-Quad was funded by a non-repayable grant, with the condition that any profit be donated. Proceeds were donated to Cradle to Crayons, a nonprofit in Newton, MA that provides clothing, school supplies, and essentials to children in need.
